story_text.value:
I made this ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake which comes out in 17 days. I remember the feeling of playing it as a kid but I hadn’t kept up with the story so I built a timeline to catch up before the Door of Time reopens.

Nintendo’s own timeline is the authority here (Hyrule Historia and their chronicle page). The fun part was rethinking how to visualize it. It branches at the end of Ocarina into three eras depending on whether Link wins or loses, so each era is its own thread on the cloth. The threads meet again much later with Breath of the Wild.

I had a lot of help from Claude. I’d often thought about building things like this but never found the time between the day job and the rest of life.

Anyone else get a lot of dumb scam calls?

These days I mostly get them on my mobile. I used to just ignore them, but then I got fed up and built a bot that answers my calls and wastes their time.

I can also steer it from Telegram mid-call.

story_text.value:
Here you have 13 different rocket engine technologies, 9 have flown, 3 built and test fired, but not flown and 1 never completed.

I created this site because I wanted to learn more about rocket engines and how they work. My background is HVAC/plumbing engineer and 3D artist, not rocket engineer, so I built this just out of my personal curiosity.

Here you can investigate each motor type and learn what each part does, explode and cutaway the model and see how fuel and oxidizer flow to generate the thrust.

Site is created using Claude Opus 5.5. Claude made also the 3D models using Blender MCP. Site runs on Babylon.js 9.16.1 on WebGL2.

What I did was basically art direction and fact checking. It took me about one week, among other projects, to get this site finalized so that I was happy about the design and outcome.

Any improvements, corrections and comments are welcome!

title.value: Show HN: A 3D catalog of rocket engines you can take apart

Hi again!

Existing text to speech or ebook to audiobook apps usually rely on KokoroTTS and don't process the pdf in a reliable way, so it often ends up reading all the front matter/opening section OCR artifacts and other crap in a machine-sounding voice. My app first fixes the content structure using an LLM and then uses heavier models to get voices with natural intonation across more than 40 languages.

About a year ago when I posted this it was still just an idea, now its becoming a real thing. Any feedback appreciated.

story_text.value:
I noticed that a lot of non-technical people don’t use AI to its full extent. Like they use the wrong model for the task, the wrong reasoning effort, or vague prompts. That gap between "what the AI can do" and "what people actually get" is what I wanted to fix.

So I spent the last two years in my spare time building a consumer AI product that tries to fix this issue.

This is how it works: When it receives the request, an LLM decides the task type (chat, reasoning, coding, writing) and the tool calls that are needed (web search, image generation, video generation, audio generation). Then it routes it to a suitable model and applies a prompt based on the task type. If it's a media generation task, it rewrites the prompt into a detailed one using prompt formulas (the prompt formulas for specific styles are mentioned in the system prompt). The LLM that is used for answering the request can also use a map, generate a mermaid diagram, generate a quiz or flashcards, generate files, etc.

A limitation right now is that routing adds latency, but I'm currently experimenting with decision-models like Jev, PPLX Decider, etc. and might use decision-models to route to the right LLM and give the tool calls like web search and media generation to the answering LLM.

It launched this week, so it's still early and I will keep improving it and adding new things.

Also sign-up/in is required to prevent abuse.

I’d really like honest feedback: what’s confusing, what’s missing, etc.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I built Connecting Captions, a live captioning and translation overlay for macOS that runs entirely on-device. Nothing goes over the network: no API calls, no audio leaving your machine, and it keeps working offline.

I wanted live translation I could use in meetings and conversations without worrying about connectivity, latency spikes, or sending sensitive audio to a third party.

The technically interesting part is a low-latency, self-correcting pipeline for speech-to-text and translation. It has two modes:

Sentence mode: buffers until a sentence boundary, then translates with full context. It’s more accurate, especially between languages with different word order. Streaming mode: translates word by word as speech arrives, trading grammatical accuracy for minimal delay.

Current state:

Platform: macOS Models: Whisper Latency: ~200 ms Languages: 25

Code: https://github.com/chrisswimlee/connectingCaptions

I’d love feedback, especially on the self-correction approach and which use cases matter most to people.

story_text.value:
At a dinner party with other parents recently, the conversation turned to the challenges we all have with communication coming from our children's schools. Emails and Texts and App notifications, coming from Teachers, Admins, PTA, After-Care programs. Overlapping information, buried key details, verbose fluff. An avalanche of text every day that must be carefully parsed to find important info.

This seems to be a universal problem and certainly one I experience every day. So literally before dinner was over I built the first version of this site on my phone with Claude.

I think the main problem is that the folks who are responsible for communication just don't have the tools and experience to know what good communication really looks like, or the parents perspective hasn't been demonstrated to them to give them more empathy. So I am hoping this can help. Feel free to share if you have the same problem with your school.

title.value: Show HN: Parents Inbox – Communication Guide for Schools
